clue.text: In tears, beg chap desperately for some respite

indicators.note: acting desperately means flailing about wildly, so the letters before it are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A tearful man begs desperately for a moment's relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desperately' rearranges all fourteen letters of IN TEARS BEG CHAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A short pause to recover or think is a period of respite, an idiom from catching one's breath.

clue.text: Having a hearty appetite no good, getting very thin

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letter for good is taken away

parts.note: someone with a hearty appetite is greedy

explanation.surface: A big eater who has lost their appetite is wasting away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no good' removes G from GREEDY.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed is a slender stem, so something reedy is tall and thin, as in a reedy figure.

clue.text: Writer achieving gold with mythical character

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
Thor is the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: A novelist strikes gold with a legendary hero.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of books is called an author, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: They bring in the crops and criminally starve her son

indicators.note: doing something criminally means doing it wrongly, so the letters of the phrase are bent into a new order

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Farmhands who gather the harvest wickedly let a mother and son go hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminally' rearranges STARVEHER, then S for son goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm workers or machines that gather ripe crops at harvest time are named for that job.

clue.text: Town produced nothing up north

indicators.note: produced means made or worked up, so the letters of the word before are made into a new word

explanation.surface: A northern town that never produced anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced' rearranges TOWN. 'up north' tells you the definition is a northern English dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: In northern English dialect the word for zero or not anything is this, as in 'you get nowt for nowt'.

clue.text: Concession managed by old singer

parts.note: a sop is a small concession made to placate someone
ran, as in ran a business, means managed

explanation.surface: An old singer is granted a small favour by management.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest female voice in classical music, and the vocalist who sings that part.

clue.text: Reduction of stewed bat eaten with first bit of Marmite

indicators.note: stewing churns ingredients together, so these letters are cooked into a new order
the first bit of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A grim recipe: a bat, stewed and eaten with a dab of Marmite, the British yeast spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stewed' rearranges BATEATEN together with M, the 'first bit of' Marmite.
explanation.definitionFit: An abatement is a lessening or cutting down, as in a tax abatement or noise abatement.

clue.text: This sounds a lot like Cockney grinding up rusty hinges with ale

definitions.text: This sounds a lot like Cockney

indicators.note: grinding something up breaks it into pieces, so the letters are crushed and remixed

explanation.surface: A grating noise of rusty hinges and ale that a listener likens to a London accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grinding up' rearranges RUSTYHINGES and ALE together. Cockney is the working-class accent of East London.
explanation.definitionFit: The accent of south-east England spoken along the Thames shares many Cockney features such as glottal stops.

clue.text: One setting off fireworks — maybe Stephenson?

definitions.meaning: a device or person that fires off a skyrocket
George Stephenson's Rocket was a famous early steam locomotive, so he launched the Rocket

explanation.surface: A firework display wonders whether its organiser might be Stephenson.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephenson's Rocket of 1829 was the pioneering railway engine; the question mark flags the punning second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A weapon or tube for firing projectiles; also, jokingly, whoever introduced a locomotive called the Rocket.

clue.text: Forcefully take charge: it should increase the score

definitions.meaning: to topple a ruler and seize power by force
in cricket, a fielder's throw that misses the stumps lets the batters run extra runs

explanation.surface: A coup that, ironically, should boost the tally.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, an overthrow is a return throw that gets past the fielders, so the batters can take extra runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Toppling a government by force is the verb sense; the cricket noun adds runs to the batting side.

clue.text: Factory scheme requires time

parts.note: a scheme is a plan

explanation.surface: A factory project is going to take a while.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial premises where goods are made are called a manufacturing plant, a synonym for works.

clue.text: Oh, Keely — in trouble? I may see you through this

definitions.text: I may see you through this

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disarray, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone calls out to a woman named Keely, worried she is in difficulty, and promises to watch over her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges OHKEELY. 'see you through' reads as support but means peering through a door's lock.
explanation.definitionFit: The small hole in a door's lock is where a nosy person may peep at someone on the other side.

clue.text: Strong wind on northern area reveals mineral deposit

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

explanation.surface: A storm over a northern region uncovers a seam of ore.
explanation.definitionFit: Galena is the natural ore of lead, a grey crystalline mineral of lead sulphide.

clue.text: Figures sit back during study of bodies at rest

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so the reversed word goes inside the other

parts.note: statics is the branch of mechanics dealing with bodies at rest

indicators.note: back says the word sit is written in reverse

explanation.surface: Physics students' numbers sit idle while they study motionless objects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' gives ITS, and 'during' puts it inside STATICS, after STAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerical data collected and analysed are called figures, a common synonym.

clue.text: Potato possibly cut underground

indicators.note: cut means trimmed short, so the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: a potato is an example of a tuber

explanation.surface: A potato chopped and buried in the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' removes the last letter, R, from TUBER. The definition is a noun: London's Underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: London's metro system is popularly called the Tube after its round tunnels.

clue.text: Type of missile, large, is found in sea

indicators.note: found in says the following letters sit inside the sea's name

parts.note: the Baltic is a sea in northern Europe

explanation.surface: A big missile has turned up in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' is the container signal: the sea opens up to take large and is. 'Type of missile' reads as a noun but the answer is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballistic missile is one that follows a free-falling arc after its powered launch phase.

clue.text: Get paper, perhaps, from halt on eastern railway

parts.note: a halt is a small railway station

explanation.surface: Buying a newspaper at a stop on an eastern line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper' looks like a newspaper but is writing paper. A halt is a minor stop on a British railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing materials such as paper, envelopes and pens are collectively known by this name; paper is one example.

clue.text: Say similar-sounding sounds?

parts.note: the clue itself repeats its opening S sounds, showing the very device it describes

explanation.walkthrough: The clue demonstrates itself: 'Say similar-sounding sounds' strings together words beginning with S.
explanation.definitionFit: This verb means to start successive words with the same consonant sound, as poets often do.

clue.text: The Yorkshire motive may be seen as disloyalty

parts.note: in Yorkshire dialect 'the' is clipped to t'
a motive is a reason

explanation.surface: A Yorkshireman's motive turns out to be betrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire speech famously shortens 'the' to t', as in 'down t' pit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Betraying one's country or sovereign is the gravest form of disloyalty.

clue.text: Bowl over in test underarm

indicators.note: in says the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Cricket: an underarm delivery in a test match shocks everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' and 'test' suggest cricket, where underarm bowling is now banned; the definition means to astonish.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowl someone over is an idiom for astonishing or overwhelming them, just as to daze them.

clue.text: Gap giving view of French lake and one French area?

parts.note: lac is the French word for lake
un is French for one

explanation.surface: A break in the hills gives a view over a French lake and a stretch of countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: A lacuna is a missing portion or blank space, especially in a manuscript or argument.

clue.text: Being arrested, knight became ill

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
ailed means fell sick

explanation.surface: A knight fell sick while he was being taken into custody.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for caught or collared by the police, as in the cops finally got him.

clue.text: Charlie in holiday footwear? That's a disgrace

indicators.note: in says the first letter is placed inside the footwear

parts.note: a sandal is open shoe worn on holiday
Charlie is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for C

explanation.surface: Someone called Charlie wearing sandals on holiday is thought shameful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts C inside SANDAL. 'Charlie' looks like a name but stands for the letter C.
explanation.definitionFit: An outrageous affair that brings shame is a source of public disgrace.

clue.text: Building style of party with Republican in charge

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: A party's architecture, with a Republican running things.
explanation.definitionFit: The plainest of the classical Greek architectural orders, with simple fluted columns.

clue.text: Thought that's within: inside, always

indicators.note: within says the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A notion that is held inside one, always.
explanation.walkthrough: 'within' points into 'inside, always', where the letters run across the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion or concept formed in the mind is a thought, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Dislikes sending back a portion of Lebanese tahini

indicators.note: sending back says the hidden letters are read backwards
a portion of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diner returns a serving of Lebanese sesame paste they disliked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a portion of' picks SETAH from the end of Lebanese and start of tahini; 'sending back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest or loathe something is a stronger form of disliking it.

clue.text: A quid sir, and I will mix up cocktails

indicators.note: mixing up stirs things together, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A bartender offers to mix drinks for a pound, sir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will mix up' rearranges AQUIDSIR and I. A quid is British slang for a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum, lime and sugar shaken together make these classic Cuban cocktails.

clue.text: In survey, I can see orcas swimming round northern tip of Newfoundland

indicators.note: round says the rearranged letters go around the two letters that follow
swimming means moving about freely, so the letters are set loose into a new order
the tip of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: On a survey trip, a whale-watcher spots killer whales swimming off Newfoundland's northern tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' gives RECOAISSANCE; 'round' wraps it about two Ns, one for northern and one the 'tip of' Newfoundland.
explanation.definitionFit: A military or exploratory survey of ground to gather information before acting.
